L134: ## 【14†1.】 【15†Introduction】
L135: 
L136: This document defines an architecture, a base set of extensible message structures, and associated flows to make signed content transparent via VDSs maintained by corresponding transparency services. The goal of the transparency enabled by the Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust (SCITT) architecture is to enhance auditability and accountability for single-issuer signed content (statements) that are about supply chain commodities (artifacts).【98†¶】
L137: Registering signed statements with a Transparency Service (TS) is akin to a notarization procedure. TSs confirm a policy is met before recording the statement on the ledger. The SCITT ledger represents a linear and irrevocable history of statements made. Once the signed statement is registered, the TS issues a receipt.【99†¶】
L138: Similar approaches have been implemented for specific classes of artifacts, such as Certificate Transparency (CT) [【100†RFC9162】]. The SCITT approach follows a more generic paradigm than previous approaches. This "content-agnostic" approach allows TSs to be either integrated in existing solutions or an initial part of new emerging systems.
L139: Extensibility is a vital feature of the SCITT architecture, so that requirements from various applications can be accommodated while always ensuring interoperability with respect to registration procedures and corresponding auditability and accountability. For simplicity, the scope of this document is limited to use cases originating from the software supply chain domain.
L140: However, the specification defined is applicable to any other type of supply chain statements (also referred to as "value-add graphs"), for example, statements about hardware supply chains.【101†¶】
L141: This document also defines message structures for signed statements and transparent statements, which embed CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) receipts [【102†RFC9942】], i.e., signed Verifiable Data Structure Proofs (VDP). These message structures are based on the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Standard [【103†STD94】] and corresponding signing is facilitated via the COSE Standard [【104†STD96】].
L636: TSs can leverage VDSs that only retain cryptographic metadata (e.g., a hash) rather than the complete Signed Statement as part of an in-depth defensive approach to maintaining confidentiality. By analyzing the relationship between data stored in the TS and data stored in Adjacent Services, it is possible to perform metadata analysis, which could reveal the order in which artifacts were built, signed, and uploaded.【351†¶】
L637: ## 【60†9.】 【61†Security Considerations】
L638: 
L639: SCITT provides the following security guarantees:【352†¶】
L640: 
L641:   1. Statements made by Issuers about supply chain Artifacts are identifiable and can be authenticated.【353†¶】
L642:   2. Statement provenance and history can be independently and consistently audited.【354†¶】
L643:   3. Issuers can efficiently prove that their Statement is logged by a TS.【355†¶】
L644: The first guarantee is achieved by requiring Issuers to sign their Statements. The second guarantee is achieved by proving a Signed Statement is present in a VDS. The third guarantee is achieved by the combination of both of these steps.【356†¶】
L645: 
L646: In addition to deciding whether to trust a TS, Relying Parties can use the history of registered Signed Statements to decide which Issuers they choose to trust. This decision process is out of scope of this document.【357†¶】
L647: ### 【62†9.1.】 【63†Ordering of Signed Statements】
L648: 
L649: Statements are signed prior to submitting to a SCITT Transparency service. Unless advertised in the TS Registration Policy, the Relying Party cannot assume that the ordering of Signed Statements in the VDS matches the ordering of their issuance.【358†¶】
L650: ### 【64†9.2.】 【65†Accuracy of Statements】
L651: Issuers can make false Statements either intentionally or unintentionally; registering a Statement only proves it was produced by an Issuer. A registered Statement may be superseded by a subsequently submitted Signed Statement from the same Issuer, with the same subject in the `CWT Claims` protected header. Other Issuers may make new Statements to reflect new or corrected information.
L652: Relying Parties may choose to include or exclude Statements from Issuers to determine the accuracy of a collection of Statements.【359†¶】
L653: ### 【66†9.3.】 【67†Issuer Participation】
L654: 
L655: Issuers can refuse to register their Statements with a TS or selectively submit some but not all the Statements they issue. It is important for Relying Parties not to accept Signed Statements for which they cannot discover Receipts issued by a TS they trust.【360†¶】
L656: ### 【68†9.4.】 【69†Key Management】
L657: 
L658: Issuers and TSs MUST:【361†¶】
L659: 
L660:   * carefully protect their private signing keys【362†¶】
L661:   * avoid using keys for more than one purpose【363†¶】
L662:   * rotate their keys at a cryptoperiod (defined in [【234†RFC4949】]) appropriate for the key-algorithm and domain-specific regulations【364†¶】
L663: #### 【70†9.4.1.】 【71†Verifiable Data Structure】
L664: 
L665: The security considerations for specific VDSs are out of scope for this document. See [【102†RFC9942】] for the generic security considerations that apply to VDSs and Receipts.【365†¶】
L666: #### 【72†9.4.2.】 【73†Key Compromise】
L667: It is important for Issuers and TSs to clearly communicate when keys are compromised so that Signed Statements can be rejected by TSs or Receipts can be ignored by Relying Parties. TSs whose receipt signing keys have been compromised can roll back their Statement Sequence to a point before compromise, establish new credentials, and use the new credentials to issue fresh Receipts going forward. Issuers are encouraged to follow existing best practices if their credentials are compromised.
L668: Revocation strategies for compromised keys are out of scope for this document.【366†¶】
L669: #### 【74†9.4.3.】 【75†Bootstrapping】
L670: 
L671: Bootstrapping mechanisms that solely rely on Statement registration to set and update registration policy can be audited without additional implementation-specific knowledge; therefore, they are preferable. Mechanisms that rely on preconfigured values and do not allow updates are unsuitable for use in long-lived service deployments in which the ability to patch a potentially faulty policy is essential.【367†¶】
L672: ### 【76†9.5.】 【77†Implications of Media Type Usage】
L673: 
L674: The Statement (scitt-statement+cose) and Receipt (scitt-receipt+cose) media types describe the expected content of COSE envelope headers. The payload media type (content type) is included in the COSE envelope header. [【104†STD96】] describes the security implications of reliance on this header parameter.【368†¶】
L675: 
L676: Both media types describe COSE_Sign1 messages, which include a signature and therefore provide integrity protection.【369†¶】

L34: # Replayable Authority Histories for Auditing Automated Agents
L35: ## 【12†Abstract】
L36: Software agents act on authority that changes while they run: permissions are granted and revoked, running instances are replaced, and some requests are refused. Activity logs record what a system reports it did, but they do not by themselves show what an agent was allowed to do when it acted, and the operator can edit them.
L37: This document specifies a model for an authority history: an append-only, signed record of who granted what to whom, which actions were admitted, which requests were refused, and which unfinished duties survive when one agent replaces another. Given independently authenticated owner keys and history identity, a verifier can replay the history and recompute its recorded authorization decisions while trusting neither the agent nor the operator.
L38: The document states what such a verifier can and cannot establish. Optional profiles cover external anchoring, federated operation, human-attested keys and zero-knowledge disclosure. An informative appendix describes one encoding.【13†¶】

L720: ## 【138†12.】 【139†Optional zero-knowledge proofs】
L721: An instantiation MAY provide zero-knowledge proofs over an authenticated history, so that a useful fact can be checked while the records establishing it stay private: a disclosed field authenticated, a private delegation chain shown to satisfy an authority or lineage predicate, or an aggregate shown to follow from committed histories. This document selects no mandatory proof system.

RFC 10070: Updates to OAuth 2.0 JSON Web Token (JWT) Client Authentication and Assertion-Based Authorization Grants (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10070.html)
【turn701825view2】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: find({"ref_id":"https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10070.html","pattern":"sole"}); Total lines: 488
L99: This specification updates the affected OAuth specifications to address the security vulnerability that was identified. Specifically, it eliminates former choices in the audience values of tokens sent to OAuth 2.0 authorization servers. 【64†Section 3.3†rfc-editor.org】 of [【65†RFC8414】] requires that the client having retrieved the metadata validates the returned issuer value.
L100: Other endpoint values of the metadata cannot be directly validated and, if used as the audience when sent to a different endpoint, can open an attack vector.【66†¶】
L101: A general description of the updates made is to require that the issuer identifier URL of the authorization server, as defined in [【65†RFC8414】], be used as the sole value of the audience of the JWT client authentication assertion. Furthermore, the authorization server rejects any JWT client authentication assertion that does not contain its own issuer identifier as the sole audience value.
L102: An explicit type for the JWT client authentication assertion, as defined in [【67†RFC8725】], is also defined to facilitate distinguishing between tokens produced in accordance with specifications published prior to these updates and those incorporating them. Specific updates made to each affected specification follow.【68†¶】
L103: ### 【20†1.1.】 【21†Notational Conventions】
L104: 
L105: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [【69†RFC2119】] [【70†RFC8174】] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.【71†¶】
L106: ### 【22†1.2.】 【23†Terminology】
L107: 
L108: All terms are as defined in the following specifications: "The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework" [【72†RFC6749】], "Assertion Framework for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication and Authorization Grants" [【73†RFC7521】], and "JSON Web Token (JWT)" [【58†RFC7519】].【74†¶】
L109: ## 【24†2.】 【25†Updates to RFC 7521】
L110: 
L111: This section updates "Assertion Framework for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication and Authorization Grants" [【73†RFC7521】] to tighten its audience requirements.【75†¶】
L112: 
L113: The description of the Audience parameter in 【76†Section 5.1†rfc-editor.org】 of [【73†RFC7521】] (Assertion Metamodel) is replaced as follows.【77†¶】
L114: 
L115: OLD:【78†¶】
L116: > Audience
L117: >     A value that identifies the party or parties intended to process the assertion. The URL of the token endpoint, as defined in Section 【79†3.2†rfc-editor.org】 of OAuth 2.0 [【72†RFC6749】], can be used to indicate that the authorization server is a valid intended audience of the assertion.
L172: > The JWT MUST contain an "aud" (audience) claim containing a value that identifies the authorization server as an intended audience. The token endpoint URL of the authorization server MAY be used as a value for an "aud" element to identify the authorization server as an intended audience of the JWT. The authorization server MUST reject any JWT that does not contain its own identity as the intended audience.
L173: In the absence of an application profile specifying otherwise, compliant applications MUST compare the audience values using the Simple String Comparison method defined in Section 【80†6.2.1†rfc-editor.org】 of RFC 3986 [【81†RFC3986】]. As noted in Section 【104†5†rfc-editor.org】, the precise strings to be used as the audience for a given authorization server must be configured out of band by the authorization server and the issuer of the JWT.【113†¶】
L174: NEW:【114†¶】
L175: > The JWT MUST contain an "aud" (audience) claim containing a value that identifies the authorization server as the intended audience. Two cases are differentiated:【115†¶】
L176: >
L177: >   1. For the authorization grant, the client is responsible for ensuring that the audience of the JWT assertion is appropriate for the authorization server to which it is sent. An authorization server MAY be identified by either its issuer identifier or its token endpoint URL.【116†¶】
L178: >
L179: >   2. For client authentication, the "aud" (audience) claim value MUST use the issuer identifier [【65†RFC8414】] of the authorization server as its sole value. The authorization server MUST have an issuer identifier to be used with this specification. The "aud" claim value MUST indicate only the issuer identifier of the intended authorization server as the audience of the JWT; this includes that the token endpoint URL of the authorization server MUST NOT be used as an audience value.
L180: The authorization server MUST reject any JWT that does not contain its issuer identifier as its sole audience value.【117†¶】
L181: >
L182: > In the absence of an application profile specifying otherwise, applications MUST compare the audience values using the Simple String Comparison method defined in 【80†Section 6.2.1†rfc-editor.org】 of [【81†RFC3986】].【118†¶】
L183: In 【119†Section 3.2†rfc-editor.org】 of [【108†RFC7523】] (Client Authentication Processing), the following requirement is added:【120†¶】
L184: > Client authentication JWTs SHOULD be explicitly typed by using the "typ" header parameter value "client-authentication+jwt" or another more specific explicit type value defined by a specification profiling this specification.【121†¶】
L185: >
L186: > The introduction of strong typing for JWTs (using explicit "typ" values) serves as a signal to distinguish between tokens produced in accordance with specifications published prior to these updates and those incorporating them. However, the primary security protection comes from the tightened audience requirements. The use of explicit typing enables clients to signal their compliance with the requirements herein.
L187: However, since strong typing alone does not prevent the attacks described in [【61†private_key_jwt.Disclosure】] and [【62†Audience.Injection】], it is NOT RECOMMENDED for servers to reject JWTs that do not have explicit types. Such rejection would cause interoperability issues with clients that already conform to the tightened audience requirements but have not yet adopted explicit typing.
L188: This approach balances security signaling with practical deployment considerations, avoiding disruption to client deployments that already conform to the tightened audience requirements but have not yet adopted explicit typing.【122†¶】
L189: In 【123†Section 4†rfc-editor.org】 of [【108†RFC7523】] (Authorization Grant Example), the sentence below is replaced as follows.【124†¶】
L190: 
L191: OLD:【125†¶】
L192: 
L193: > The intended audience of the JWT is "https://jwt-rp.example.net", which is an identifier with which the authorization server identifies itself.【126†¶】
L194: 
L195: NEW:【127†¶】
L196: 
L197: > The intended audience of the JWT is "https://authz.example.net", which is the authorization server's issuer identifier.【128†¶】
L198: In the same section, the JWT Claims Set example is replaced as follows.【129†¶】
L199: 
L200: OLD:【130†¶】
L201:

L269: ## 【32†5.】 【33†Updates to RFC 9126】
L270: 
L271: This section updates "OAuth 2.0 Pushed Authorization Requests" [【145†RFC9126】] to tighten its audience requirements.【146†¶】
L272: 
L273: The last paragraph in 【147†Section 2†rfc-editor.org】 of [【145†RFC9126】] (Pushed Authorization Request Endpoint), which describes the audience value, is replaced as follows.【148†¶】
L274: 
L275: OLD:【149†¶】
L276: > Due to historical reasons, there is potential ambiguity regarding the appropriate audience value to use when employing JWT client assertion-based authentication (defined in 【150†Section 2.2†rfc-editor.org】 of [【108†RFC7523】] with private_key_jwt or client_secret_jwt authentication method names per Section 9 of [【151†OpenID.Core】]). To address that ambiguity, the issuer identifier URL of the authorization server according to [【65†RFC8414】] SHOULD be used as the value of the audience.
L277: In order to facilitate interoperability, the authorization server MUST accept its issuer identifier, token endpoint URL, or pushed authorization request endpoint URL as values that identify it as an intended audience.【152†¶】
L278: NEW:【153†¶】
L279: > Due to historical reasons, there is potential ambiguity regarding the appropriate audience value to use when employing JWT client assertion-based authentication (as defined in 【150†Section 2.2†rfc-editor.org】 of [【108†RFC7523】] and as updated by 【154†Section 4】 with the "private_key_jwt" or "client_secret_jwt" authentication method names per Section 9 of [【151†OpenID.Core】]).
L280: To address that ambiguity, the issuer identifier URL of the authorization server according to [【65†RFC8414】] MUST be used as the sole value of the audience. The authorization server MUST reject any such JWT that does not contain its own issuer identifier as the sole audience value.【155†¶】
L281: >
L282: > Client authentication JWTs SHOULD be explicitly typed by using the "typ" header parameter value "client-authentication+jwt" or another more specific explicit type value defined by a specification profiling this specification.【156†¶】
L283: >
L284: > The introduction of strong typing for JWTs (using explicit "typ" values) serves as a signal to distinguish between tokens produced in accordance with specifications published prior to these updates and those incorporating them. However, the primary security protection comes from the tightened audience requirements. The use of explicit typing enables clients to signal their compliance with the requirements herein.
L285: However, since strong typing alone does not prevent the attacks described in [【61†private_key_jwt.Disclosure】] and [【62†Audience.Injection】], it is NOT RECOMMENDED for servers to reject JWTs that do not have explicit types. Such rejection would cause interoperability issues with clients that already conform to the tightened audience requirements but have not yet adopted explicit typing.
L286: This approach balances security signaling with practical deployment considerations, avoiding disruption to client deployments that already conform to the tightened audience requirements but have not yet adopted explicit typing.【157†¶】
L287: ## 【34†6.】 【35†Operational Considerations】
L288: Changes in this specification affect interoperability between clients and authorization servers that implement different versions. In particular, the resulting compatibility is not entirely symmetric. A client implementing this specification will interoperate with both authorization servers conforming to the updates herein as well as authorization servers implementing earlier versions.
L289: However, some clients implementing earlier versions may not interoperate with authorization servers that strictly enforce the updated requirements in this specification. Deployments upgrading to this specification should consider this asymmetry when planning rollouts or migrations, as it may be necessary to ensure that clients are updated before, or in coordination with, authorization servers that enforce the updated behavior.【158†¶】
